name: Alexamorelin
lead: Alexamorelin is a synthetic heptapeptide growth hormone secretagogue, related to hexarelin, with the sequence Ala-His-D-2-methyl-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2. A 2000 study reported its endocrine activities in humans [6].

It has not been approved as a medicine. It appears in the scientific literature mainly as one of the growth hormone releasing peptides (GHRPs) that anti-doping laboratories screen for in urine [1][3][4]. It is named among the prohibited peptides covered by sports drug-testing methods [3][4].
No published trials have tested it for any appearance or muscle-related outcome.

For physique and appearance communities, interest in compounds of this type comes from the idea that raising growth hormone could support lean mass and fat loss; in alexamorelin's case the published record consists of one early physiology study and a series of anti-doping analytical papers rather than studies of body composition.[6][3]
infobox: Included in peptide screening panels for sports drug testing [3][4]

paras: Alexamorelin is a heptapeptide built with unnatural D-amino acids, in the same design family as hexarelin, ipamorelin and the GHRP series, which were derived from met-enkephalin analogues and designed for their ability to stimulate growth hormone release.[5] A 2025 toxicology paper describes it as mimicking ghrelin by binding the growth hormone secretagogue receptor type 1a (GHS-R1a) in the pituitary, which promotes endogenous GH release.[7]

The same study predicted 21 single-reaction metabolites by computer and tested human hepatocyte incubations; N-acetylation was the main predicted and identified transformation, and the work aimed to find consumption biomarkers for doping control.[7] These analytical papers also note that orally active peptides of this type can raise endogenous GH while escaping the standard test for exogenous GH, which is why dedicated assays were built.[1]

The first and only human endocrine study dates from 2000.[6] Since the early 2010s, sports drug-testing laboratories added alexamorelin to multi-peptide screens, and the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list was cited in 2016 as covering alexamorelin along with other GHRPs, ipamorelin, hexarelin and related small peptides.[4] The compound is not marketed as an approved medicine in the literature reviewed.

Doping-control papers describe how new, potentially performance-enhancing compounds are often distributed through internet platforms before their metabolism is characterised, which motivated work on GHRP metabolism and urine screening.[2] The assays developed reach detection limits of 50 to 500 pg/mL, below the 2 ng/mL minimum performance level used in sports testing.[4]

sections.h: Place in the growth hormone secretagogue family
paras: Growth hormone secretagogues are a drug class that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone. Reference summaries divide them into agonists of the ghrelin receptor, which include hexarelin (also called examorelin), GHRP-2, GHRP-6, ipamorelin and the non-peptide ibutamoren, and agonists of the growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor such as sermorelin, CJC-1295 and tesamorelin.[9] Alexamorelin belongs to the first group, which is why it is studied alongside hexarelin.[6]

Many members of the class also raise prolactin, cortisol and IGF-1 to varying degrees.[9] The main established clinical application of the class is the assessment and treatment of growth hormone deficiency.[9]

sections.h: Why the appearance angle is indirect
paras: Interest in compounds of this type in physique communities rests on a chain: more circulating growth hormone, then higher IGF-1, then effects on lean mass, fat mass and recovery. For alexamorelin that chain has not been tested in any published study; the only human data measure hormone release over a few hours in six volunteers.[6] Its relative hexarelin has a longer research history, and reference summaries record that it reached phase II studies for growth hormone deficiency and heart failure without being marketed, and that with prolonged use its growth hormone response has been reported to diminish partially and reversibly.[10]

sections.h: Hormonal effects reported in the human study
paras: In the 2000 comparison with hexarelin, alexamorelin raised growth hormone and prolactin and also stimulated ACTH and cortisol, with the cortisol-axis response to the higher alexamorelin dose larger than that after hexarelin, and aldosterone also rose.[6] Hexarelin itself is described as giving small, dose-dependent increases in prolactin, ACTH and cortisol.[10] These co-released hormones are part of why researchers describe such peptides as less selective than some newer analogues.
The only identified human study is a 2000 report of its endocrine activities as a synthetic GH secretagogue [6]. No trials of muscle, body-composition or cosmetic outcomes were found.

The 2000 study in the European Journal of Endocrinology enrolled six young adults and compared alexamorelin with hexarelin, the best-studied peptide of the group. Both produced dose-dependent increases in growth hormone and prolactin after intravenous administration, and both raised ACTH and cortisol. The ACTH and cortisol responses to the higher alexamorelin dose were significantly larger than those after hexarelin, and aldosterone rose after alexamorelin but not hexarelin. The report also assessed GH release after oral administration.[6]

The same paper noted that alexamorelin inhibits GHS binding in vitro and that its endocrine activity had not been studied in humans before.[6] No longer-term, body-composition or safety trials have been published.

Alexamorelin is listed among growth hormone releasing peptides for which urine screening assays have been developed, because such orally active peptides can raise endogenous GH while escaping the standard test for exogenous GH [1][3]. Mass-spectrometry methods for these peptides have been refined repeatedly [2][4][5].

A 2025 study used human hepatocyte incubations to identify metabolites that could serve as markers of alexamorelin consumption [7]. A 2026 workflow paper includes peptidic doping agents in blood matrices [8].

timeline.event: Alexamorelin included in peptide doping-screening methods [1][3][4].
Metabolite markers of consumption identified in vitro [7].
Metabolism and nano-LC screening methods for GHRPs published.[2][3]
High-throughput LC-MS/MS screen covers alexamorelin in equine and human urine.[5]

card.summary: An obscure hexarelin-related GH secretagogue peptide known mostly from anti-doping screening papers; no appearance trials exist.
card.note: Not an approved medicine; listed in doping-control peptide panels.

quick.overview:
Alexamorelin is a lab-made peptide that stimulates growth hormone release, related to hexarelin. It is discussed mainly in sports anti-doping research.

One 2000 human study described its hormonal effects; no study has tested it for muscle or looks outcomes.
quick.mechanism: As a growth hormone secretagogue, it is described as raising the body's own GH output rather than supplying GH itself [3].
quick.risks: No safety data from clinical trials were found. It is covered by sports drug-testing screens and is not an approved drug.
